scroll-reveal.title: Scroll Reveal
scroll-reveal.ratingLabel: core for bento · minimalism · neo-brutalism · flat · hand-drawn
scroll-reveal.blurb: Elements animate in as they cross the scrollport. The most-used scroll effect on the web, and the cheapest to get right.
scroll-reveal.markup:
entry 10% → cover 38%

Finishes well before centre screen. This is the working default.

entry 0% → cover 100% — too slow

Still animating when it is halfway up the screen, which reads as sluggish. The range is the whole craft.

No stagger logic

Each element's position in the scrollport is the stagger.

Scrubbed

Scroll up and it plays backwards.

Composite-only

opacity and transform, nothing else.

The end

Scroll back up — nothing is left half-revealed.
scroll-reveal.craft:
animation-range is the whole craft. Left at its default (cover) the element is still animating when it is halfway up the screen, which reads as sluggish. entry 10% cover 38% finishes it early. The second card above is deliberately set to the sluggish range so the difference is visible rather than described.

No stagger logic is needed. Each element's position in the scrollport is the stagger — which is why a CSS reveal on a grid costs nothing while a JS one needs batching.

Scrubbed vs triggered. CSS view() is scrubbed by default: scroll up and it plays backwards, and nothing is ever left half-revealed. Triggered (IntersectionObserver, or ScrollTrigger without scrub) is better when the motion has personality — a bounce or an overshoot — that should not run in reverse.
avoid: Above the fold. Content in the initial viewport should already be there.
On every element. If everything reveals, nothing is emphasised and the page feels laggy.
On text the user is trying to read while scrolling.
scroll-reveal.packs: ● for bento (staggered across cells — the signature entrance), minimalism (one technique for the whole page, opacity-led, short travel), neo-brutalism (snap, not float — short distance, linear, no bounce), flat and hand-drawn (paired with a per-element rotation). ⚠ for neumorphism, and the constraint is specific: never start a low-contrast control at opacity: 0. ⚠ for brutalism — permitted only with linear timing and no fade, or better, steps(1).

scroll-progress.title: Scroll Progress
scroll-progress.ratingLabel: core for swiss · editorial · modernism · flat
scroll-progress.blurb: A bar that fills as the document scrolls. The cheapest technique in the catalogue, and the only one WCAG exempts from reduced motion.
scroll-progress.markup:
Two indicators, one timeline

The bar at the top and the ring at the bottom right are both bound to scroll(root block). Neither reads the scroll position in JavaScript; both are driven by the compositor.

This is the only technique in the catalogue that survives reduced motion. WCAG 2.3.3 exempts motion that conveys position, and a progress indicator conveys nothing else. Collapse it and you have removed information rather than decoration.

Why the bar is a transform

It scales on the X axis from a left origin. Animating width would produce the same picture and force layout on every frame — the exact failure engine.md §6 exists to prevent.

The ring uses stroke-dashoffset with pathLength="1", which normalises the path so the offset runs cleanly from 1 to 0 regardless of the circle's real circumference.

Keep scrolling

Both indicators track the document, so they reach 100% exactly when this page ends.

A progress bar is also the honest fallback for a pack where almost every other technique is ✗. It costs nothing, it breaks nothing, and it is genuinely useful.

Swiss uses it as a solid red bar four to eight pixels tall, straight out of the poster vocabulary. Editorial uses it because the reading indicator was invented for exactly this content.

Scroll to the bottom and watch both hit full.
scroll-progress.craft:
This is the one technique that survives prefers-reduced-motion. WCAG 2.3.3 exempts motion that conveys position; engine.md §6 states the exception in as many words. Collapsing a progress bar removes information, not decoration.

Scale, never width. The bar animates transform: scaleX() from a left origin. Animating width looks identical and forces layout every frame.

pathLength="1" on the ring normalises the SVG path so stroke-dashoffset runs 1 → 0 without anyone computing a circumference.
avoid: On a short page. If there is nothing to track, the bar is decoration pretending to be information.
As a second progress signal alongside a step indicator — pick one.
Collapsed under reduced motion. It is exempt, and removing it removes information.
scroll-progress.packs: ● for swiss (a solid red bar, 4–8px, from the poster vocabulary), editorial (the reading indicator was invented for this content), modernism (a bar is a Bauhaus object) and flat. Safe everywhere else — this is the technique with no ✗ in the matrix.

parallax.title: Parallax
parallax.ratingLabel: core for glassmorphism · hand-drawn — and ✗ for seven packs
parallax.blurb: Layers move at different rates to imply depth. The most contradicted technique in the catalogue: seven of the twelve packs ban it outright.
parallax.mechanism: CSS scroll() timeline on a fixed layer
parallax.markup:
The backdrop is the effect

The fixed layer behind this panel is the only thing moving. Everything else scrolls normally — which is the whole trick.

Why scroll(), not view()

A backdrop is position: fixed, and a fixed element never enters or leaves the viewport — so view() progress never advances and nothing moves. This is the single most common way a CSS parallax silently does nothing.

Seven packs ban this

Parallax contradicts flat by definition, swiss because layers place elements off-grid every frame, modernism because illusory depth has no structural role, and neumorphism on first principles — one surface colour means there are no layers.

And the pairing that works

Glass over a moving backdrop is the signature pairing in the entire matrix. It is also the most dangerous: backdrop-filter re-blurs every frame. Three glass panels here, and never on a repeating list item.
parallax.craft:
A backdrop is fixed, so it needs scroll() and not view(). A fixed element never enters or leaves the viewport, so view-progress never advances — the animation registers, reports running, and moves nothing. This was a live bug in this repo before the audit caught it.

Do not set an explicit animation-range on a scroll() timeline unless you mean it. scroll() already spans the document; writing 0% 100% collapses to a zero-length range and nothing moves.

The moving layer must be behind everything. If a parent paints its own background over the fixed layer, the parallax is hidden behind a static copy of itself.
avoid: Any pack that bans depth — flat, swiss, modernism, neumorphism, bento, brutalism, minimalism.
On a repeating scroll item behind glass. backdrop-filter re-blurs every frame; that is the documented FPS killer.
Without the scale(). A translated backdrop reveals its own edges unless it is oversized.
parallax.packs: ● for glassmorphism — the backdrop is what glass is for, and this is the strongest pairing in the matrix — and hand-drawn, where doodle layers at different depths are natural. ⚠ for neo-brutalism (hard-offset flat planes only, never soft atmospheric depth) and skeuomorphism. ✗ for seven packs, each for its own reason.

pinned-scene.title: Pinned Scene
pinned-scene.blurb: A full-bleed stage holds while content passes through it. ONE visual, held — not a sequence of steps.
pinned-scene.markup:
scroll-state(stuck: top) — this label turns green when the bar sticks
one stage · held · full bleed

The stage holds. Content passes through it.

This is not the two-column layout scrollytelling uses. The pinned element is the full viewport, and the content scrolls over it.

One visual, unchanged

That is the distinction from scrollytelling. A pinned scene holds a single visual while the page moves past it. Scrollytelling swaps the visual at each step — the visual is the argument's illustration, and it changes as the argument does.

Built from position, nothing else

No timeline, no listener, no library. It holds because its containing block is taller than it is — and it lets go when that block ends.
pinned-scene.craft:
How this differs from scrollytelling. A pinned scene holds one visual while content passes; scrollytelling swaps the visual at each step. Same underlying position: sticky, opposite intent — and they should not share a layout, which is why this one is a full-bleed stage rather than a column beside text.

The track must be substantially taller than the pinned element. A composition requirement, not a CSS one, and the commonest reason a pin reads as broken.

Never animate the pinned element itself. GSAP's docs say it plainly — it throws off the measurements. Animate its children.

scroll-state(stuck: top) replaces the listener. Chrome 133+ answers "is it stuck" in CSS, at scroll composition time. Before it, every sticky-shadow effect on the web was a banned scroll listener.
avoid: When the adjacent column is shorter than the pinned element — the pin will barely hold.
With overflow:hidden on any ancestor. It kills sticky. Use overflow-x:clip instead.
On mobile, where a pinned element can eat most of a short viewport.
pinned-scene.packs: ● for editorial (a sticky image with text scrolling beside it is a magazine spread), modernism (a composition that assembles itself from square, circle and triangle) and bento (pin the grid, animate the cells' contents). ✗ for neumorphism — a component style has nothing at page scale to pin.
pinned-scene.ratingNote: contrast with scrollytelling, which swaps the visual per step

stacking-cards.title: Stacking Cards
stacking-cards.blurb: Panels stick in sequence and pile up at the top of the viewport. Built entirely from sticky offsets.
stacking-cards.mechanism: position: sticky with an incremental offset
stacking-cards.markup:
01

Each panel sticks at a hard offset

18px per panel, not a smooth ramp. The offsets are visible and countable, which is the point — the mechanism is not hidden.

02

The shadow does the depth

Because the shadow has no blur, a panel landing on the one beneath reads as two solid planes rather than a soft pile.

03

No-shrink variant

Nothing scales and nothing fades. A scale() would round the corners optically and undo the pack; a fade is banned outright by it.

04

Built from position, not JavaScript

This is position: sticky and one custom property. No scroll listener, no library, no measurement on every frame.
stacking-cards.craft:
The offset is a custom property, not four hand-written values. top: calc(12vh + var(--i) * 18px) means adding a fifth panel is one attribute, and the ramp cannot drift out of sequence.

The no-shrink variant is the one to reach for. The common version scales each panel down as the next arrives. That softens corners optically — which is fine for a rounded pack and destructive for a hard-edged one — and it is motion that must then collapse under reduced motion. Sticky alone collapses to nothing because nothing was moving.

The wrapper needs trailing space. Without padding-bottom the last panel unsticks the instant it arrives.
avoid: With a scale or fade under reduced motion — sticky alone has nothing to collapse; added motion does.
On more than four or five panels. Past that the stack occupies more scroll than it earns.
In brutalism. Stacking is polish, and the pack rates it ✗.
stacking-cards.packs: ● for neo-brutalism — a 4px 4px 0 hard shadow makes the stack's depth explicit and literal in a way a soft shadow cannot — and bento, where cells and cards share a geometry. ✗ for brutalism, which rates it as polish.

scroll-snap.title: Scroll Snap
scroll-snap.ratingLabel: core for modernism · skeuomorphism · swiss · flat · neo-brutalism
scroll-snap.blurb: The scroll port comes to rest on defined positions. Native browser behaviour — no timeline, no library, no listener.
scroll-snap.risk: medium — it takes control of scroll
scroll-snap.markup:
One panel at a time

The scroll port rests on each panel. scroll-snap-stop: always means a fast flick cannot skip one.

Native, not animated

No timeline, no library, no listener. This is scroll-snap-type: y mandatory and nothing else.

Which one is snapped?

The inactive panels are dimmed by scroll-state(snapped: y) — in CSS. This was the single most hand-rolled scroll listener on the web.

mandatory vs proximity

mandatory always lands on a snap point. proximity only snaps when you stop nearby, which is far safer for content of varying height.
scroll-snap.craft:
This is native behaviour, and that is the whole appeal. It costs nothing, it runs off the main thread by definition, and there is no fallback to write because unsupported browsers simply scroll normally.

mandatory is a commitment. It always lands on a snap point, which means a panel taller than the viewport becomes unreachable in its middle. Use proximity when panel heights vary.

scroll-state(snapped: y) answers "which one is active" in CSS. Chrome 133+. It needs three elements: the scroll container with scroll-snap-type, the target with both scroll-snap-align and container-type: scroll-state, and a child that carries the query. The queried element cannot be the container itself.
avoid: With panels taller than the viewport under `mandatory` — their middles become unreachable.
On a reading page. Snapping fights reading, which is why editorial rates it ✗.
Alongside smooth scroll. Two systems competing for the scroll position is a guaranteed fight.
scroll-snap.packs: ● for modernism — the strongest conceptual match anywhere in the matrix, because the style is built on a module and snap moves in modular steps — plus skeuomorphism (physical controls detent; a dial clicks into position), swiss, flat and neo-brutalism. ⚠ for hand-drawn: snapping is precise and that pack's method is "order first, chaos later". ✗ for editorial — snapping fights reading.

horizontal-scroll.title: Horizontal Scroll
horizontal-scroll.ratingLabel: core for swiss · modernism · neo-brutalism · flat
horizontal-scroll.blurb: A track that scrolls sideways. Native overflow beats a hijacked vertical scroll every time.
horizontal-scroll.markup: ↔ drag, shift+wheel, or swipe · more to the right →
horizontal-scroll.craft:
Native overflow beats a hijacked vertical scroll. The pinned-and-translated version — where scrolling down moves a track sideways — takes the page's scroll away, breaks keyboard navigation and confuses the scrollbar. Real overflow-x gives you touch, trackpad, keyboard and a real scrollbar for nothing.

scroll-state(scrollable: right) makes the affordance honest. Most horizontal tracks show a permanent "→" that lies at the end of the list. This one queries whether there is anything left to scroll, in CSS, and hides itself when there is not.

Give the track vertical padding, not the cards. A focus ring on a card inside an overflow container is clipped unless there is room for it.
avoid: As a hijacked vertical scroll. It steals the page's scroll and breaks the scrollbar.
Without a visible affordance. A track that looks like a cut-off row reads as a bug.
For primary navigation. Sideways content is discovered less than vertical content.
horizontal-scroll.packs: ● for swiss and modernism (movement along the grid's own axes, in modular steps), neo-brutalism and flat. Useful in bento and editorial for a single strip. Note the CSS carousel primitives — ::scroll-button() and ::scroll-marker, Chrome 135+ — now generate accessible controls for exactly this, reported as a tablist, with no JavaScript.

scrollytelling.title: Scrollytelling
scrollytelling.blurb: A sticky visual holds while text scrolls beside it, and the visual changes at each step. Content sequencing, not a visual device.
scrollytelling.markup:
STEP 01
STEP 02
STEP 03
STEP 04

The visual holds, the text moves

The panel on the left is position: sticky. Each figure inside it is bound to its own step's view progress, so the visual changes as the argument does.

It is content sequencing

Scrollytelling is not an effect bolted onto a page. The steps are the structure — which is why the technique file calls it narrative rather than a visual device.

The column must be much taller

Each step is 78vh here. If the text column is not substantially taller than the sticky panel, the pin barely holds and the whole thing reads as a glitch.

Steps, not a continuous scrub

Each figure crossfades over its own step rather than one animation running the length of the piece. That keeps a step readable while it is on screen.
scrollytelling.craft:
How this differs from a pinned scene. A pinned scene holds one visual while content passes. Scrollytelling changes the visual at each step — four figures here, each bound to its own step's progress. The visual is the argument's illustration, so it has to move when the argument does.

The steps are the structure. This is the one technique in the catalogue where the content model comes first: you are writing a sequence of claims, and the visual answers each one. Reaching for it without that sequence produces a sticky image and some paragraphs.

Each step owns its own timeline. One animation spanning the whole piece would leave the visual mid-transition while a step is being read. Per-step view() ranges with a hold in the middle (18% → 82% here) keep each state stable while its text is on screen.

The fallback must show something. With every step at opacity: 0, an unsupported timeline leaves an empty box. Showing the first figure is a valid degraded state; an empty panel is not.
avoid: Without a real step sequence. Otherwise it is a sticky image with paragraphs next to it.
When the text column is shorter than the sticky visual — the pin will not hold.
For content the reader may want to skim. Each step demands a full scroll.
scrollytelling.packs: ● for editorial — this style is long-form narrative, and a sticky image with text beside it is literally a magazine spread — and hand-drawn (illustrated narrative). ✗ for neumorphism: a component style has nothing at page scale to pin.

text-reveal.title: Text Reveal
text-reveal.ratingLabel: core for editorial — and ✗ for skeuomorphism
text-reveal.blurb: Words or lines brighten as the block crosses the scrollport. Display type only, never body copy.
text-reveal.markup:
Type that arrives as you reach it, one word at a time.

This is display type only. The same effect on body copy makes the reader wait for the page to permit them to read, which is the fastest way to make a site feel broken.

Each word carries its own view() range, so no JavaScript splits the text at runtime — though the words do have to be wrapped in spans by the template.

Note the resting opacity is .16, not 0. Unrevealed words stay faintly visible, so the shape of the sentence is legible before it resolves and a screen-reader user is never presented with an empty block.

One more, further down.

Scroll back up and the words fade out again — a scrubbed reveal is reversible, which is what keeps it from ever leaving a sentence half-lit.
text-reveal.craft:
Display type only. Editorial rates this ● for pull quotes and display headlines and explicitly never for body copy. A reader who has to scroll to be allowed to read is being obstructed by the design.

Never start at opacity: 0. The resting state here is .16 so the sentence's shape is visible before it resolves. It also means a failed timeline degrades to faint rather than to blank.

Skeuomorphism rates this ✗ on principle — type in that style is printed, engraved or embossed onto a material, so it cannot fade in without contradicting the material it is part of.
avoid: On body copy. Editorial rates it ● for display and pull quotes only.
Starting at opacity:0 — it makes the failure mode a blank block.
In skeuomorphism, where type is part of the material and cannot fade in.
text-reveal.packs: ● for editorial, on pull quotes and display headlines only. ✗ for skeuomorphism — printed and engraved type cannot fade in. Use sparingly everywhere else: it is the technique most likely to be experienced as an obstruction.

svg-path-draw.title: SVG Path Draw
svg-path-draw.ratingLabel: core for hand-drawn — its signature technique
svg-path-draw.blurb: A line draws itself as you scroll. The one technique that legitimately animates stroke-dashoffset.
svg-path-draw.markup:
pathLength="1" is the trick

It normalises the path so stroke-dashoffset runs cleanly from 1 to 0, with no one computing a real path length in JavaScript.

Several paths, one range

Each path carries its own pathLength, so they draw together regardless of how different their real lengths are.

The one legitimate exception

stroke-dashoffset is on engine §6's banned list because it forces paint. This is the technique that cannot exist without it — so it is exempted explicitly, and the audit records the exemption rather than hiding it.
svg-path-draw.craft:
pathLength="1" is the whole trick. It normalises any path to a length of 1, so stroke-dasharray: 1; stroke-dashoffset: 1 works on every path in a drawing without measuring a single one. Without it you need path.getTotalLength() in JavaScript.

This technique is the exception to §6's composite-only rule. stroke-dashoffset forces paint on every frame — it is on the banned list by name. The exemption is declared in the section's data-composite-exempt, so the audit reports it as a known exception rather than silently passing it.

Paint cost scales with stroke complexity. A handful of simple paths is fine; a detailed illustration re-rasterises every frame.
svg-path-draw.snippet:
<path d="…" pathLength="1"/>     <!-- normalise, so no JS measuring -->

.draw path{
  fill: none;
  stroke-dasharray: 1;
  stroke-dashoffset: 1;
  animation: dw auto linear both;
  animation-timeline: view();
  animation-range: entry 5% cover 55%;
}
@keyframes dw{ to{ stroke-dashoffset: 0 } }

@supports not (animation-timeline: view()){
  .draw path{ stroke-dashoffset:0; animation:none }
}
avoid: On a detailed illustration. Every frame re-rasterises the stroke.
For content that must be readable. A half-drawn line is not information.
Without pathLength — otherwise every path needs measuring in JavaScript.
svg-path-draw.packs: ● for hand-drawn, where it is the signature technique: a hand-drawn mark that draws itself is the technique restating the style, and arrows, circles and underlines are already SVG paths. ● for editorial on rules, dividers and illustrated marginalia.

scroll-theme-shift.title: Scroll Theme Shift
scroll-theme-shift.ratingLabel: core for flat — and ✗ for neumorphism
scroll-theme-shift.blurb: The page's colours change as you scroll. Solid swaps only; the moment it becomes a gradient it is a different technique.
scroll-theme-shift.markup:
Ink to primary, as you cross

One solid value interpolating to another. No gradient, no blur — which is exactly why flat rates this ● and why it costs almost nothing.

The contrast moves with it

This is the trap. Text must clear contrast at both ends of the range and everywhere between. Shifting from a light ground to a dark one leaves white text at 1.15:1 for the first half — a real failure caught by the audit on this repo's own flat page.

Give it a base colour

With keyframes alone the element is transparent until the timeline resolves, so text lands on the page ground for a frame. Declare the from colour as a real background.
scroll-theme-shift.craft:
The contrast changes with the background, so it must be checked across the whole range — not at one end. A shift from the page ground to a primary leaves white text unreadable for the first half of the scroll. Shift dark → dark, or light → light, and the text stays legible throughout.

Always declare the from colour as a real background. With keyframes alone the element is transparent until the timeline resolves; text then sits on the page ground for a frame, and any contrast check sees the wrong pair.

Neumorphism rates this ✗ and the reason is mechanical: its dark shadow is the surface × 0.87 and its light shadow is the surface + 13%. Animate the background and both shadows become wrong, so the extrusion inverts or vanishes mid-scroll.
avoid: Shifting between a light and a dark ground with fixed text colour — contrast breaks mid-range.
In neumorphism, where both shadows are derived from the surface and would need recomputing every frame.
As a gradient. A soft fade is a different technique and most packs that allow this one ban that.
scroll-theme-shift.packs: ● for flat — solid colour swaps with no gradients are exactly what the style is made of. ✗ for neumorphism (both shadows derive from the surface) and minimalism, which bans a second visual event. Note this is one of two techniques that legitimately animate a non-composite property; it is cheap because background-color paints without layout.

scroll-marquee.title: Scroll Marquee
scroll-marquee.ratingLabel: core for brutalism — its one core technique
scroll-marquee.blurb: A ticker that moves with the scroll rather than on a clock. Motion that admits it is motion.
scroll-marquee.markup:
NO EASING ◆ NO RADIUS ◆ NO BLUR ◆ DEFAULT LINK BLUE ◆ NATIVE CONTROLS ◆ NO EASING ◆ NO RADIUS ◆ NO BLUR ◆ DEFAULT LINK BLUE

Scroll-bound, not clock-bound. A CSS marquee on an infinite loop runs whether anyone is there or not. This one only moves when you do — which makes it honest about being a response to the reader rather than ambient decoration.

It is also the reason this survives in a pack that bans nearly every other technique. <marquee> was a 1995 HTML element; a scroll-bound ticker is its descendant, and brutalism's whole thesis is that the browser's own history is the material.

REVERSED ◆ SECOND TRACK ◆ OPPOSITE DIRECTION ◆ REVERSED ◆ SECOND TRACK ◆ OPPOSITE DIRECTION ◆ REVERSED

Two tracks running opposite ways is the common pairing. Keep the travel modest — -42% here — because a marquee that outruns its own content shows the gap.
scroll-marquee.craft:
Duplicate the content, then travel less than half of it. The run must contain enough repeats that translating it never exposes the end. Travelling -42% of a double-length run keeps a full copy on screen at all times.

Scroll-bound beats clock-bound. An infinite CSS loop animates whether or not anyone is looking, costs frames continuously, and has to be collapsed entirely under reduced motion. A scroll-bound marquee stops when the reader stops.

This is brutalism's only ● entry, and that is not an accident: stacking, parallax, video and text reveal are all rated ✗ as polish, while a ticker is machinery.
avoid: As an infinite clock-bound loop — it burns frames with nobody watching.
With travel greater than the duplicated content, which exposes the gap.
In minimalism, which rates it ✗: perpetual motion in a style built on stillness.
scroll-marquee.packs: ● for brutalism — its only core entry, because stacking, parallax, video and text reveal are all rated ✗ as polish while a ticker is machinery. ✗ for minimalism: perpetual motion in a style built on stillness.

smooth-scroll.title: Smooth Scroll
smooth-scroll.ratingLabel: ✗ for brutalism · neo-brutalism · swiss — and never the default
smooth-scroll.blurb: Inertial, lerped scrolling. The only technique here that changes how the whole page feels rather than how one element behaves.
smooth-scroll.mechanism: a library that hijacks native scroll
smooth-scroll.markup:
This section deliberately does not demonstrate the effect. Smooth scroll is global: enabling it here would change how every other section on this site behaves, and would hijack the scroll of a page whose whole purpose is to demonstrate scroll. That refusal is the demonstration.

What it actually is

A library intercepts the wheel and touch events, prevents the native scroll, and animates a transform on the page body toward the target position on a requestAnimationFrame loop. It is the one technique in this catalogue that is not a CSS scroll-driven animation and cannot be.

Why three packs ban it outright

Brutalism rates it ✗ emphatically: the browser's honest defaults are the entire thesis, so lerped scroll is the single most anti-brutalist addition available. Neo-brutalism because inertia is soft and the style is hard — its signature interaction is an instant translate(4px,4px). Swiss because the style is objective and precise, and inertia is neither.

The alternative almost nobody reaches for

You usually want smoothed animation, not smoothed scrolling. Lenis smooths the whole page's scroll position — a global feel change, and the reason this technique carries so many accessibility caveats. Anime.js sync: 0.25 and GSAP scrub: 1 smooth one animation's catch-up and leave native scroll untouched. Most of the same perceived liquidity, none of the hijack.
ApproachWhat it smoothsNative scrollReduced motion
Lenis / ScrollSmootherthe page's scroll positionhijackedmust disable entirely
Anime sync: 0.25one animation's catch-upuntouchedcollapse that animation
GSAP scrub: 1one timeline's catch-upuntouchedcollapse that timeline
CSS scroll-behavioranchor jumps onlyuntouchedhonours the media query

If you ship it anyway

Disable it entirely under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce — a lerped scroll is precisely the vestibular trigger WCAG 2.3.3 addresses. Keep the scrollbar honest, never lengthen the page to buy runway, and test keyboard paging: a hijacked scroll frequently breaks Page Down and focus scrolling.
smooth-scroll.craft:
The refusal is the point. Every other section here demonstrates its technique. This one cannot: smooth scroll is global, so enabling it would change every other page on this site and hijack the scroll of a document whose purpose is to demonstrate scroll.

Most requests for "smooth scroll" are requests for smoothed animation. That is a different thing, it is cheaper, and it does not take the page's scroll away — sync: 0.25 or scrub: 1 rather than a scroll-hijacking library.

It is the only technique here that is not CSS. Everything else in this folder runs on a compositor-driven timeline. This one is a requestAnimationFrame loop, permanently.
avoid: As a default. It is a deliberate, global, high-risk choice.
In brutalism, neo-brutalism or swiss — all three rate it ✗ for stated reasons.
Without a reduced-motion escape. A lerped scroll is a vestibular trigger.
Alongside scroll snap. Two systems fighting for the scroll position.
smooth-scroll.packs: ✗ for brutalism, neo-brutalism and swiss, each for a reason rooted in the style rather than in taste. ⚠ everywhere else — permitted, never assumed. There is no pack in the catalogue for which this is a core fit.

video-scrub.title: Video Scrub
video-scrub.ratingLabel: ⚠ everywhere · ✗ for flat — the heaviest payload in the catalogue
video-scrub.blurb: Scroll position drives which frame of a real sequence is shown. 48 frames, 214 KB, and not one line of JavaScript.
video-scrub.mechanism: stacked frames, one view() slice each
video-scrub.cost: high — the asset is the cost
video-scrub.markup:
This is a real asset. Forty-eight WebP frames of a machined part on a turntable, rendered to disk and shipped — 214 KB, about 4.5 KB a frame. Scroll the stage below and the sequence scrubs.

It also runs on no JavaScript at all, which the technique doc did not expect. Each frame is stacked and given its own one-forty-eighth slice of a view() timeline with steps(1). Frames turn on in order, later ones painting over earlier ones, and turn off again in reverse when you scroll back up.

48 frames · 214 KB · CSS only

The asset is still the cost. That is the honest lesson and it has not changed: this sequence is small because the subject is simple and procedurally rendered. Real footage at this frame count runs to megabytes, and that is before anyone asks for retina.

ApproachPayloadScrub quality
Frame sequence (used here)every frame ships — 214 KB for 48exact, no decode stalls
Video + currentTimesmallerseeks to keyframes; stutters unless keyframe-dense
Video + WebCodecssmallerexact, but a real engineering commitment

Why a sequence beat the video here. A normally-encoded video seeks only to keyframes, so a scrub lands on the nearest one and stutters. Encoding for scrub — a keyframe every frame or two — can multiply the file size past what the sequence costs. And a sequence needs no JS, because there is no currentTime to set.

Flat rates this ✗, and the reasoning is exact: the heaviest possible payload, in the style whose entire pitch is lightness.
video-scrub.craft:
Frames turn on, they do not cross-fade. Each frame gets a hairline slice of the timeline and steps(1,end), with fill: both. Before its slice it is transparent; after it, opaque. Later frames sit above earlier ones in the DOM, so the newest visible frame wins — and scrolling back up switches them off in reverse.

The slice is computed, not written 48 times. --slice: calc(100% / var(--n)) and an inline --i per frame. Adding frames is a count change, not a rewrite.

This turned out not to need JavaScript. The technique doc assumes JS because currentTime is a media property no CSS can reach. A frame sequence has no currentTime — so it runs entirely on the compositor, which is strictly better than the documented approach.

First frame eager, the rest lazy. Otherwise 48 requests fire before anything paints.

The timeline belongs to the tall wrapper, not the frames. The frames sit inside a sticky stage that never traverses the viewport, so their own view() progress never advances — the animation registers, reports running, and shows frame zero forever. This is the same failure as putting view() on a fixed parallax layer, and it is the single most common way a CSS scrub silently does nothing.
avoid: In flat — it rates ✗: the heaviest payload in the style whose pitch is lightness.
On mobile data without a poster-only fallback.
With every frame eager-loaded — 48 parallel requests before first paint.
As decoration. If the footage is not the content, the payload is not justified.
video-scrub.packs: ⚠ everywhere it is permitted, ✗ for flat and brutalism. ○ for minimalism — this is Apple's model, and it is what makes "Apple does video scrub inside a minimal shell" coherent rather than contradictory. Confirm the asset budget before proposing it.

scroll-world.title: Scroll World
scroll-world.ratingLabel: ● for glassmorphism only — and it carries a per-build cash cost
scroll-world.blurb: Technique plus generated art direction, sold as one unit. It owns the ground layer — sky, horizon, light and terrain — which is what separates it from plain video scrub.
scroll-world.mechanism: generated frame chain on a view() timeline
scroll-world.cost: cash — ~$27 per six-scene chain at production quality
scroll-world.markup:
Forty frames of a camera pushing through a diorama. Rendered to disk — 203 KB — and scrubbed by the same CSS mechanism as video scrub. Glass chrome sits over it, because that is the one pack this technique composes with rather than overwrites.

Note what the frames carry: sky, sun, horizon, terrain and light. That is the whole distinction from plain video scrub — scroll-world owns the ground layer, which is why packs that also own the ground are overwritten by it.

Chrome over a world

Glass composes with this because it is chrome, not ground. Bento, flat, skeuomorphism and hand-drawn all own their own ground — two grounds cannot coexist.

These frames are procedural, not photoreal. The shipping form of this technique is a chain of generated photoreal scenes: roughly N image plus 2N−1 video generations, mobile doubling the video count, about $27 for a six-scene 1080p chain. What is above demonstrates the mechanism and the layer relationship honestly at zero cash cost. ROUTER Gate 3.5 still requires confirming that budget before proposing the real thing.

Which packs it composes with

RelationshipPacksWhy
Composesglassmorphism ● · minimalism ○ · editorial ○chrome packs — they sit on a world without claiming to be one
Overwrittenskeuomorphism · neumorphism · flat · bento · hand-drawn · brutalismthese own the ground themselves; two grounds cannot coexist
Conditionalneo-brutalism ⚠ · modernism ⚠ · swiss ⚠hard chrome over a rendered world works, but fights the style's flatness

The runtime alternative. A real 3D scene — react-three-fiber with drei on React, @threlte/core plus @threlte/theatre on Svelte — driven by a scroll progress value. No per-build generation cost at all; a WebGL bundle and a GPU budget instead. engine.md §6 applies: never mix GSAP or Three.js with Motion in one component tree, because they fight over the same frames.
scroll-world.craft:
It owns the ground layer. That is the real distinction from video scrub, and it is what decides pack compatibility: the frames above carry sky, horizon and light, so a pack that supplies its own ground has nowhere to stand. Chrome packs compose; ground packs are overwritten.

Same CSS mechanism as video scrub — stacked frames, one steps(1) slice each, no JavaScript. The cost difference is entirely in what the frames contain.

The cash cost is real and applies to the production form. Procedural frames like these cost nothing; a photoreal generated chain is ~$27 for six scenes, and ROUTER requires confirming that before the technique is proposed. It is the only item in the catalogue with that condition.
avoid: Without confirming the cash cost of the production form. ROUTER requires it, uniquely here.
In a pack that owns its own ground — skeuomorphism, neumorphism, flat, bento, hand-drawn, brutalism.
Mixed with Motion in one component tree, if using the 3D runtime form.
scroll-world.packs: ● for glassmorphism alone — the only style in the catalogue for which that is true, because glass is chrome over a world rather than a world itself. ○ for minimalism and editorial. Overwritten in the six ground-owning packs; ⚠ in the three where hard chrome over a rendered world is conditional.

view-transition.title: View Transition
view-transition.ratingLabel: the one entry with no ✗ in the matrix
view-transition.blurb: Motion between views rather than within a scrolling page. The one technique here that is not a scroll technique — which is exactly why it fills a hole.
view-transition.binding: triggered by navigation or a DOM change
view-transition.markup:
Click a tile. The tile and the detail panel share a view-transition-name, so the browser morphs one into the other — it is not a crossfade, it is the same element in two places.

DETAIL

Opened without a route change, a library, or a single line of animation code — document.startViewTransition() and one shared name.

checking support…

Why this is in a scroll folder. Every other technique here animates while you scroll. This one animates when you arrive — and the corpus had no entry for it at all. For a narrative that spans routes, page-to-page motion was the missing half.

Cross-document needs no framework and no JavaScript: two lines of CSS give a multi-page site animated navigation.
view-transition.craft:
Names must be unique per document. Two elements sharing a view-transition-name throws rather than degrading — which is why the demo above assigns the name to the clicked tile only, and clears it afterwards.

Reduced motion is not automatic. This is page-level motion under §6 and needs the same treatment as parallax: strip every name, or branch in JS and update the DOM directly. The "update without a transition" button above takes that second path.

It has the best failure mode in this folder. Where the API is unsupported the DOM simply updates instantly — the web working normally. Compare that to a reveal stuck at opacity: 0.

It is the honest answer for brutalism and neumorphism, the two packs where nearly every scroll technique is ✗. A navigation transition is not a scroll effect, so the objection to scroll polish does not reach it.
avoid: On every navigation. A transition on a link followed fifty times becomes friction.
To disguise a slow load — it animates the arrival, it does not make it sooner.
With a duplicate view-transition-name. It throws rather than degrading.
view-transition.packs: The one entry with no ✗ in the matrix, because it operates on a different axis from everything else here. It is the honest answer for brutalism and neumorphism, where nearly every scroll technique is ✗ — a navigation transition is not a scroll effect. Keep it to steps(1) or no easing in brutalism.
